## What is Machine Learning?

- The short version:

  + machine learning (ML) is a subset of statistical learning that focuses on prediction

- The longer version:

  + ML is the idea of constructing data-driven algorithms that *learn*, rather than *assume*, the mapping between predictor variables and response variable(s)

  + we suppose no parametric form for the mapping *a priori*, even if technically one can write one down *a posteriori* (for example, by translating a tree model to a indicator-variable-filled mathematical expression)

  + linear regression, for instance, is not an ML algorithm since we can write down the linear equation ahead of time, but (we'll see that) a random forest is an ML algorithm since we've no idea what the number of splits will end up being in each of its individual trees

## Machine Learning: Which Algorithm is Best?

.pull-left[

- That's actually not the right question to ask

- The right question is ask is: why should I try different algorithms?

  + because you (generally) cannot visualize the distribution of predictor variables in their native space

  + the performance of different algorithms is predicated on how predictor data are distributed, e.g., 

- The picture to the right shows data for which there are two predictor variables (along the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis) and for which the response variable is binary: "x"s and "o"s

  + an algorithm that places linear boundaries or that segments the plane into rectangles will do well given the data to the left

  + whereas, an algorithm that places circular boundaries will fare better given the data to the right

  + "do well/fare better": will do a better job at predicting whether a new datum is actually an "x" or an "o", with consideration to the required model complexity
  
]

.pull-right[

## Your First ML Model: the Decision Tree

.pull-left[

<br>

- A decision tree is a model that segments a predictor space into disjoint $p$-dimensional hyper-rectangles, where $p$ is the number of predictor variables

  + for a regression tree, the predicted response in a hyper-rectangle is the average of the response values of the training data in that hyper-rectangle

  + for a classification tree, the predicted class in a hyper-rectangle is, by default, that class that is most represented in the training data in that hyper-rectangle
  
- Should I use this model?

  + yes: it is easy(ish) to explain to non-statisticians and easy to visualize/predict with

  + no: trees do not generalize as well as other models (i.e., they tend to have higher test-set MSEs) as they *can* suffer from high variance if not constrained
  
]

.pull-right[

<br><br><br><br>

## Decision Tree: Algorithmic Details

.center[
  ![:scale 45%](./Algorithm_8.1.png)
]

(Algorithm 8.1, *Introduction to Statistical Learning* by James et al.)

- The classification tree algorithm is similar: instead of splits based on reduction of the residual sum-of-squares (RSS), the splits would be based on, e.g., reduction of the *Gini coefficient*, a metric whose value becomes smaller as each node becomes more "pure," i.e., populated more and more by objects of a single class


---

## Decision Tree: Regression Example

.center[
  ![:scale 35%](./rss_0.png)
  ![:scale 35%](./rss_1.png)
]

- The dataset above has two predictor variables and (let's call it) a quantitative response (1, 2, or 3)

  + pre-split: $\widehat{Y} = \overline{Y} = 1.875$, with RSS = 16.625

  + post-split: $\widehat{Y}_{\rm left} = 1$ and $\widehat{Y}_{\rm right} = 2.5$ (total RSS = 3.5): the change in RSS is sufficient to accept the proposed split


---

## Decision Tree: Regression Example

.center[
  ![:scale 35%](./rss_1.png)
  ![:scale 35%](./rss_2.png)
]

- The splitting process continues separately in each new segment

  + no further proposed splits are possible to the left

  + the proposed split to the right reduces the overall RSS to zero

  + no further splits can be made at upper right or lower right: the tree-building is done


---

## Decision Tree: Caveats
  
- The decision tree algorithm is a *greedy algorithm* which implements top-down *recursive binary splitting* to build the model, so the final model may not be "globally optimal" (i.e., it may not have the smallest possible overall RSS, MCR, or Gini value)

- Overfitting is an issue: a tree that places a hyper-rectangle around each datum will be highly flexible (with training set MSE or MCR equal to zero!), but will not generalize well (very poor testing set performance)

  + a strategy to mitigate overfitting is to grow a large tree, then apply *cost complexity* (or *weakest link*) pruning


---

## Decision Tree: Example - Fitting

- Our dataset has 25 predictor variables and a response variable that is a binary celestial object type: 385 galaxies and 243 stars

  + we do a 70-30 split of the dataset to create training/test sets
  
```{r echo=FALSE}
file.path = "https://github.com/FSKoerner/F25-36600-data/raw/refs/heads/main/rosat_classify.Rdata"
load(url(file.path))
rm(file.path)
w            <- which(response == "GALAXY  " | response == "STAR    ")
df           <- data.frame(predictors[w, ], "class" = response[w])
df$class     <- as.character(df$class)
w            <- which(df$class == "GALAXY  ")
df$class[w]  <- "GALAXY"
df$class[-w] <- "STAR"
df$class     <- factor(df$class)
suppressMessages(library(tidyverse))
df %>% dplyr::select(., -Z_BEST) -> df
df$class <- droplevels(df$class)
set.seed(909)
s        <- sample(nrow(df), round(0.7 * nrow(df)))
df.train <- df[s, ]
df.test  <- df[-s, ]
```

```{r warning=FALSE}
library(rpart)
rpart.out  <- rpart(class ~ ., data = df.train)
class.prob <- predict(rpart.out, newdata = df.test, type = "prob")[, 2]
class.pred <- ifelse(class.prob > 0.5, "STAR", "GALAXY")
round(mean(class.pred != df.test$class), 3)
table(class.pred, df.test$class)
```

- A classification tree does much better than simply classifying all the data as galaxies!  (I.e., the "null MCR" is 0.387)

## Decision Tree: Example - Interpreting

.pull-left[

- Interpretation is done via examination of the tree

  + test-set prediction is done by sending each test-set datum "down" the displayed tree and seeing where it ends up
  
```{r eval=FALSE,fig.width=6,fig.height=6,fig.align="center"}
library(rpart.plot)
rpart.plot(rpart.out, extra = 104)
# Re: "extra" - see the rpart.plot documentation
```

]

## Decision Tree: Example - Pruning

.pull-left[

- From the `plotcp()` documentation: a "good choice of `cp` for pruning is often the leftmost value for which the mean lies below the horizontal line"

  + here, that would be 0.045, which corresponds to 5 leaves

```{r eval=FALSE,fig.width=4,fig.height=4,fig.align="center"}
plotcp(rpart.out)
```

]

.pull-right[

```{r echo=FALSE,fig.width=6,fig.height=6,fig.align="center"}
plotcp(rpart.out)
```

]


---

## Decision Tree: Example - Pruning

```{r}
rpart.pruned <- prune(rpart.out, cp = 0.045)
class.prob   <- predict(rpart.pruned, newdata = df.test, type = "prob")[, 2]
class.pred   <- ifelse(class.prob > 0.5, "STAR", "GALAXY")
round(mean(class.pred != df.test$class), 3)
table(class.pred, df.test$class)
```

- The pruned tree's MCR is the same than the unpruned tree's MCR, so in this case, pruning, or lack thereof, did not adversely impact the model's generalizability


---
